title: Differentiable Bit-Widths: Co-optimizing Pruning and Quantization via SVD for Ultra-Efficient LLM Compression
claim: Prior methods prune and then quantize in separate sequential steps; ours jointly learns per-component bit-widths, treating pruning as 0-bit.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, sequential steps vs unified bit-width blocks
description: Two side-by-side panels with hatched gray blocks and dashed outlines. Panel (a), 'Sequential optimization', shows step 1 pruning, where an FP16 weight is split into a kept FP16 block and dashed 'truncated' regions. Step 2 quantization then turns the kept block into INT3, with the truncated parts still dashed. Panel (b), 'Co-optimization', shows 'Differentiable Bit-Width' in red-highlighted letters. A single INT weight holds blocks labeled INT3, INT2 and truncated, plus a bit column reading 3, 2, 0 with a small flame icon marking it as learnable. Blue step labels in (a) contrast with the unified red-accented (b). Bold words in the captions draw the eye first.
caption: Our compression concept illustration. We co-optimize pruning and quantization in a single step by updating bit-widths in our differentiable method.
abstract: SVD-based pruning and quantization have recently emerged as a promising strategy for the ultra-efficient compression of large language models. In these methods, compression is performed in two stages: components are first truncated, and the remaining ones are subsequently quantized. Although this decoupled pipeline benefits from both pruning and quantization, it requires separate optimization for each stage and fails to fully exploit their balance, which can lead to suboptimal performance under aggressive compression. To address this limitation, we propose a new LLM compression method that co-optimizes pruning and quantization in a unified framework. Our key idea is a differentiable method for learning component-wise bit-widths, allowing less important components to be assigned 0-bit precision and pruned away. Notably, our method performs favorably against two-stage baselines, even when subjected to extreme quantization settings ($1.61$ bits) designed for ultra-efficiency. Code: https://github.com/MMAI-Laboratory/DBW.
